ladder.teaches: search and insert by the ordering
ladder.why: The ordering tells you which subtrees cannot contain an answer, so whole branches are skipped.

ladder.teaches: validate with lower and upper bounds
ladder.why: Checking each node against its children is not enough; carry an (low, high) interval down, or check that inorder is strictly increasing.
Inorder visits keys in ascending order, so the k-th smallest is the k-th node an iterative inorder walk pops.
With an ordering, the LCA is the first node on the way down that lies between p and q: no recursion, O(h).

ladder.teaches: search and insert by the ordering
ladder.why: Insert, search and delete written from scratch: each walks one path chosen by comparisons, and delete handles the two-child case with the successor.
Inorder traversal paused between steps: a stack of the left spine gives next() in amortised O(1).

ladder.teaches: search and insert by the ordering
ladder.why: Walking down by the ordering and remembering the last node where you turned left finds the next larger key.
Without an ordering, LCA is a post-order question: the first node whose two sides each report a target.
With parent pointers the LCA is where two root paths meet: mark one path, climb the other.

ladder.teaches: validate with lower and upper bounds
ladder.why: Rebuilding from preorder in O(n) by giving each subtree its allowed (low, high) range.
Insertion order plus the split-point idea: the LCA is the first inserted value between p and q, which avoids building a degenerate chain.
Flatten by inorder into a sorted list, then expand two pointers outward from target's insertion point.
Inorder makes every key range a contiguous slice, so prefix sums and binary search answer many queries fast.
Sortedness as a diagnostic: the one or two descents in the inorder sequence name the two swapped nodes.

ladder.teaches: validate with lower and upper bounds
ladder.why: Bounds checking done bottom-up: each subtree reports (isBST, min, max, sum) so the parent decides in O(1).

notes: Only one BST-flavoured problem in the bank comes from an OA (blackrock LCA); the practice rungs are mostly interview problems. Half the pool is unrelated 'rotation' problems (arrays, matrices, strings) matched by the word 'rotate'; they were ignored. The LCA rungs mix BST, plain-binary-tree and parent-pointer versions on purpose.
